profiles.name: chrome_131

provenance.method: derived from maintained uTLS Chrome fingerprint data
provenance.capture_note: This profile is not a first-party Chrome packet capture. It reproduces the corresponding maintained uTLS Chrome profile and must not be described as independently verified against live Chrome.

application_settings_code_point.note: Chrome 131 and earlier sent application_settings at 0x4469. Byte-identical to chrome_133 in every other respect.

citations.what: Chrome ClientHello parrot tables (extension order, cipher list, groups)
X25519MLKEM768 share layout and shared-secret order

profiles.fingerprint_sha256_covers: SHA-256 over the 'fingerprint' object serialised as JSON with sorted keys, no whitespace, and ASCII-only content, so the digest is reproducible from any language without agreeing on a non-ASCII escaping rule. Provenance and citations are excluded on purpose, so editing prose does not invalidate the vector.

record_layer_version.why: BoringSSL tls_record_version() returns TLS1_VERSION while ssl->s3->version == 0; Go crypto/tls writeRecordLocked, which uTLS inherits and Xray and sing-box run, sets vers = VersionTLS10 on the first record. RFC 8446 5.1 permits either value, so this is a parroting requirement and not a correctness one.

padding_rule.why: the ML-KEM key share puts the hello well past 0x1ff

ech_grease.aead_note: One suite, fixed. BoringSSL setup_ech_grease() picks aes_128_gcm when EVP_has_aes_hardware() and chacha20_poly1305 otherwise, so a given install always sends the same id; uTLS BoringGREASEECH() offers only {HKDF_SHA256, AES_128_GCM}. Choosing per connection would itself be a fingerprint.

profiles.name: chrome_151

provenance.method: first-party capture of the shipping browser
provenance.why_not_utls: uTLS has no table for this build. At upstream commit 23b1dac1 (2026-08-02) HelloChrome_Auto is still HelloChrome_133 and no uTLS table anywhere carries the ML-DSA signature algorithms Chromium now offers, so transcribing uTLS would reproduce a hello no shipping Chrome sends.
provenance.capture_note: First-party capture. The browser was driven headlessly on the maintainer's machine against a local listener that recorded the raw ClientHello record, and the same browser was driven again through a recording CONNECT relay to a public destination; both hellos produced the identical JA4, so the localhost capture is the hello this build sends to the internet and not a loopback special case.
provenance.measured_ja4_note: JA4 of the captured hello, and of three further hellos the same browser sent to a public destination through a recording relay -- all four identical. The computation producing it was validated against tls.browserleaks.com on a Firefox capture, hash and raw form both, character for character. chrome_133 reads t13d1516h2_8daaf6152771_d8a2da3f94cd: JA4_a and JA4_b already match, and JA4_c is where the ML-DSA schemes land.

application_settings_code_point.note: Chrome 132 and later moved application_settings to 0x44cd; Chromium 151 still sends it there. chrome_131 is the same table at the older 0x4469.

no_grease.note: Firefox GREASEs nothing. Adding GREASE for consistency with the other tables would be the tell.

key_share_reuse.rule: the standalone x25519 share repeats the X25519 half of the X25519MLKEM768 share
key_share_reuse.note: The Chromium family generates the two independently; sending one key twice there would be visible. Firefox does the opposite, so this is per profile.

ech_grease.note: Firefox differs from Chrome here: two candidate AEADs and a single payload length of 223.

profiles.name: firefox_153

provenance.method: first-party capture of the shipping browser
provenance.why_not_utls: uTLS has no table for this build. At upstream commit 23b1dac1 (2026-08-02) HelloFirefox_Auto is still HelloFirefox_148, which offers a cipher Firefox 153 dropped and omits two extensions it now sends.
provenance.capture_note: First-party capture. The browser was driven headlessly on the maintainer's machine against a local listener that recorded the raw ClientHello record, and the same browser was driven again through a recording CONNECT relay to a public destination; both hellos produced the identical JA4, so the localhost capture is the hello this build sends to the internet and not a loopback special case.
provenance.measured_ja4_note: JA4 of the captured hello, and independently the value tls.browserleaks.com reported for the same browser on the same connection -- hash and raw form both, character for character. firefox_148 reads t13d1715h2_5b57614c22b0_a54fffd0eb61: even JA4_a differs, which is the part a detector reads without hashing anything.
